title: I Used the Tandoor-Slot Hours on the Cook Who Camped My Numbered Skewers

parts.text: I stepped into the tandoor bay at 5:05 p.m. and cook Rafi was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE SLOT. THIRTY MINUTES. SKEWERS STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was twenty-nine, kitchen secretary, holding a checkout that listed our numbered skewers. Rafi shrugged. "Cooks are the clay." I photographed the board, the booking, and his leftover naan hooks on my numbered skewers. Then I asked for the slot log. At 5:13 the bay pinged why Rafi's name was on my hooks. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The bay can see Rafi's leftover naan hooks on my numbered skewers.

social.video_title: He camped my numbered tandoor skewers on my slot — Part 1/2
social.description: Tandoor bay, leftover naan hooks, a thirty-minute clock he posted. I logged the skewers. Would you have asked for the slot log?

parts.text: Rafi called it residual heat until the bay asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the hook still. The skewers went back to my numbered booking. Rafi ran a slot of his own and told the next cook atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: COOKS ARE NOT THE CLAY. I keep my skewers on a labeled rack. Rafi brown-bags his residual. The bay finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Cooks are not the clay — Part 2/2
social.description: Slot log, numbered skewers, and a second line on the board. Was residual heat ever my hooks?
